content.thinking:
The legal text of the proposition is now clear.

Prop 42 appears to restrict only state-level taxes, not local ones. The official summary and LAO confirm this. SPUR's claim that local governments would be blocked is slightly imprecise.

The phrase "authorize collection" could potentially block state laws that authorize local personal property taxes. Existing local personal property taxes in effect before December 31, 2025 are grandfathered.

The definition of personal property is extremely broad. It would ban future wealth taxes, business personal property taxes, and taxes on digital or intellectual assets.

Estate taxes likely fall outside the ban because they are transfer taxes rather than ownership taxes.

Prop 42 would also ban retroactive taxes, with only a narrow exception for legislative emergency taxes up to 365 days.

Prop 40 conflicts directly with Prop 42. Prop 40 taxes personal property ownership and applies retroactively based on residency as of January 1, 2026. If Prop 42 passes, Prop 40 would be null and void entirely.

The campaign frames Prop 42 as protecting ordinary retirement savings. This is misleading. Prop 40 explicitly exempts real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts from taxation. The claim of six separate proposals also needs verification. Section 5 reveals the measure's true purpose: nullifying competing initiatives like Prop 40.

Prop 42 is funded overwhelmingly by the billionaires who would pay Prop 40.

Deceptive framing does not automatically make a policy bad. A poison pill can still be substantively sound.

Economic evidence on wealth taxes shows most OECD countries abandoned them. France repealed its ISF in 2018 after capital flight. Sweden, Germany, Denmark, Austria, and the Netherlands also removed similar taxes. Norway and Spain still retain versions.

Switzerland maintains a longstanding cantonal wealth tax with a broad base and relatively low rates. Valuation of private businesses, illiquidity, capital flight in open economies, and high administrative costs relative to revenue are common problems. Such taxes can distort investment by favoring real estate and exempt assets over saving. Saez and Zucman argue that a well-designed wealth tax on the very rich is administrable, especially as a one-time measure, and that California has information advantages.

A one-time tax avoids behavioral distortions that annual taxes create, because taxpayers cannot change their behavior after the fact. The retroactive January 1, 2026 date was designed to prevent relocation before the tax applies.

California depends heavily on capital gains and high-income taxpayers. The top one percent pay roughly forty to fifty percent of state income tax. If billionaires relocate, the state would face significant ongoing revenue loss.

The LAO estimates Prop 40 could reduce state income tax by less than one billion dollars annually. That is modest compared to the tens of billions in one-time revenue, though uncertainty remains.

Governor Newsom and many California Democrats worry that a one-time wealth tax would set a dangerous precedent and accelerate the exodus of founders, IPOs, and venture capital. California's tech economy is mobile at the top.

Billionaires have already begun leaving. Brin claims Nevada residency. The threat of exit is being used to veto any future extreme wealth taxation.

A 5% one-time tax is small relative to recent wealth gains. Many billionaires' wealth was created using California's public infrastructure, universities, and talent pool.

The retroactive ban is the more principled part of the proposition. Retroactive taxation based on past residency is legally aggressive. The US Supreme Court has allowed some retroactive tax changes when they are rationally related to a legitimate purpose and not excessively so. State tax nexus and due process requirements still demand minimum connections.

Taxing someone who left California in February 2026 based on January 1 residency for a tax passed in November 2026 raises serious constitutional questions about dormant commerce, due process, privileges and immunities, and takings. The measure might still be struck down.

The retroactivity ban carries rule-of-law benefits. The exception for thirty-six-five-day legislative emergency taxes preserves some flexibility.

However, the retroactivity ban is specifically written to kill Prop 40's anti-avoidance design.

The retroactivity ban applies to all taxes, not just wealth taxes. It would prevent retroactive loophole closures within a tax year, which California frequently does. The thirty-six-five-day exception only covers legislative emergency statutes, not ordinary loophole fixes or initiatives.

The retroactivity ban would invalidate routine California tax practices. A new tax passed in September that applies to January income would be retroactive under the measure's definition. The thirty-six-five-day emergency exception would still permit short retroactivity during a declared fiscal emergency. Without such an emergency, new taxes must be prospective only. This is a reasonable good-government rule, though it reduces revenue flexibility.

A permanent constitutional ban on ownership taxes would make future wealth taxes impossible without another amendment. It would also bar new state taxes on personal belongings such as yachts, art, jewelry, and vehicles. Existing local vehicle and fuel taxes are grandfathered.

New vehicle taxes could be blocked if they are ownership-based. Counties currently tax business equipment, so new state-authorized business personal property taxes would likely be prohibited under the broad definition. Carbon or excise taxes probably would not be affected, since those are not ownership taxes. A mark-to-market income tax on unrealized gains might also fall within the ban.

A mark-to-market tax on unrealized gains would likely be challenged under the proposed ban, since courts might broadly interpret the ownership prohibition to cover appreciation. California currently has no state estate tax; Prop 6 in 1982 banned inheritance and gift taxes.

SPUR's claim that Prop 42 bans local taxes and real estate taxes is inaccurate. The text explicitly preserves real property taxation and limits the ban to state law. The California Democratic Party opposes Prop 42, while Governor Newsom supports it.

Labor is split on Prop 42. Firefighters, building trades, and peace officers support it. SEIU-UHW opposes it.

The campaign's warnings about ordinary retirement accounts and firefighters' pensions are misleading. Prop 40 exempts ordinary retirement accounts. The fear-mongering about taxing firefighters' pensions is not supported by the actual competing measure.

I should verify whether any historical California wealth tax proposals actually targeted ordinary retirement accounts. The campaign's warnings may be overstated.

Killing Prop 40 would remove a major revenue source for California. Federal Medicaid cuts are already creating large funding gaps in the state healthcare safety net. A one-time tax could yield tens of billions to hundreds of billions of dollars, which would materially help fill those gaps.

The LAO's conservative estimates are more credible than union projections. Even a modest one-time tax would not permanently replace the roughly nineteen billion dollars in annual Medicaid cuts. Prop 40 would serve only as a temporary bridge.

Revenue certainty remains uncertain due to avoidance strategies, valuation litigation, and stock price volatility.

A one-time five percent tax on worldwide net worth raises serious design problems. Valuing private companies such as Stripe or SpaceX is contentious and likely to generate extensive legal challenges.

A one-time tax could force founders to sell stock, risking loss of company control and market disruption. Retroactive worldwide taxation of departed residents would likely spawn years of litigation before any revenue arrives, precisely when healthcare funding is most needed. The threat also risks further exodus of entrepreneurs and venture capital.

The LAO's estimate of less than one billion dollars in annual income tax revenue loss may be too low. A broader behavioral response from high earners could exceed static projections.

European experience shows that wealth taxes were repealed because they raised little revenue relative to economic costs and were easily avoided. A one-time retroactive tax is harder to avoid than an annual tax, which is the intended design. Constitutional challenges could still undermine it.

Prop 42 would permanently restrict California's fiscal capacity. The state already faces severe structural limits from Prop 13, the two-thirds vote requirement for tax increases, and Gann spending caps. A broad constitutional ban on ownership taxes would add another layer of constraint.

The retroactivity ban is only partially justified. The thirty-six-five-day emergency exception shows the drafters already recognize some retroactivity is necessary. Courts already limit excessive retroactivity, so the broad prohibition is unnecessary to protect due process. It is also paired with a sweeping wealth tax ban that far exceeds any fairness rationale.

Voting no on Prop 42 does not impose any tax. It simply preserves the status quo and allows voters to reject Prop 40 separately without a constitutional amendment. The only unique effect of voting yes is the permanent constitutional restriction.

Prop 42 functions as an anti-democratic poison pill. It would nullify Prop 40 even if voters approve both measures, silently overriding a separate tax proposal that supporters may also favor.

The conflict clause would nullify the entire competing measure, not merely its conflicting parts. Even non-conflicting provisions in Prop 40 would be voided if Prop 42 passes with more votes. This makes the poison-pill effect more severe than initially described.

The better vote is no. Opposing Prop 40 directly does not require constitutionalizing a permanent ban. The measure is a billionaire-funded poison pill that uses misleading advertising about middle-class retirement to sell itself.

The retroactivity principle is overbroad and not worth the constitutional lock-in. Voters can already reject specific retroactive taxes at the ballot. One remaining argument for voting yes is that wealth taxes are poor economics, and opening the door would erode California's mobile tax base and hurt public services long-term.

A constitutional ban is the only reliable way to prevent repeated wealth tax attempts, since ballot measures are easier to pass than to repeal. The retroactive residency hook in Prop 40 would trap people by taxing their prior year's worldwide wealth after they have already left the state, which violates fairness regardless of who is targeted.

Voting yes on Prop 42 is the only way to guarantee a billionaire tax never takes effect if Prop 40 passes. Firefighters and building trades support it, though their backing may stem from pension-tax framing or political alliances rather than direct concern for ordinary retirement accounts. California already ranks among the highest-taxed states, so constitutional protection against a new tax category is not inherently excessive.

The argument that voters can simply reject Prop 40 directly is incomplete. A constitutional ban would permanently close the door to repeated wealth tax proposals and eliminate the uncertainty that itself drives capital flight. Newsom supports Prop 42 partly for this reason. Strategic voting based on poll projections is a separate consideration from the fundamental policy question.

The marginal decision is the constitutional ban and poison pill, not the tax itself. California's existing constitutional tax prohibitions have a poor track record of creating fiscal rigidity. Adding another layer is likely to age poorly.

The sweeping definition of personal property would create legal uncertainty for future tax policy. Prop 40 itself may be unconstitutional on its own, raising retroactivity, commerce clause, and due process concerns. Voting no also discourages deceptive ballot tactics that use conflict clauses to void other voter-approved measures.

PROPOSITION 40
Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers. Initiative Constitutional
Amendment and Statute.
ANALYSIS OF MEASURE
BACKGROUND
California Is Home to Many Billionaires. Several of the wealthiest people in the world live
in California. Wealth is the value of all the things a person owns. Wealth is different from
income, which is how much a person earns in a set period of time, like one year. A person’s
wealth typically is measured by their net worth. A person’s net worth is the value of all the
things they own, like stocks, businesses, or other investments, minus their debts. California is
home to a few hundred people with net worth over $1 billion, often called billionaires. Many of
these billionaires gained their wealth as executives or investors in California technology
companies.
Health Care Is a Major Category of State Spending. The state and federal government
spend over $200 billion per year on state health care programs. Most state health care spending is
for Medi-Cal, the state’s health insurance program for low-income people. State spending also
supports public health programs, mental health care, and drug and alcohol treatment.
PROPOSAL
Establishes One-Time Wealth Tax on Billionaires. Under Proposition 40, billionaires who
were residents of California on January 1, 2026 would have to pay a one-time state tax equal to
5 percent of their net worth. The tax would be due in 2027. Taxpayers would have the option to
spread the payments over five years but would have to pay more to do so. Real estate, pensions,
and retirement accounts generally would be excluded from the tax.
Most of the Money Must Be Spent on Health Care. The state would decide how and when to
spend the money from the wealth tax, but it would have to be spent on certain types of services.
Ninety percent of the money would have to be spent on health care services for the public. The
rest would have to be spent on education, food assistance, and administration of the wealth tax.
Existing rules in the State Constitution that limit spending and require the state to spend a certain
amount on schools and community colleges would not apply to this money.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 2 of 3
FISCAL EFFECTS
Temporary State Revenue Increase From Wealth Tax. The state probably would collect
tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax. This temporary increase in state tax collections
would be spread across several years. Exactly when and how much the state would collect is
very hard to predict for many reasons. For example, it is hard to know what actions billionaires
would take to reduce the amount of tax they pay. Also, much of the wealth is based on stock
prices, which are always changing.
Possible Ongoing Decrease in State Income Tax Revenues. California billionaires, like all
those earning money in the state, currently pay state taxes on their annual income. Billionaires
may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example,
some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the
state also would go away. These responses probably would reduce state revenues by less than
$1 billion per year. This could mean less money for the state’s General Fund, which is the
account that pays for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.
State Costs to Administer the Wealth Tax. The state would have costs to determine how
much wealth tax is owed and to collect tax payments. These costs could be tens of millions of
dollars per year for several years. These costs would be paid from the new wealth tax revenues.

A YES vote on this measure means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires
equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not collect a one-time tax from
billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST’S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT
• Temporary state revenue increase from a new wealth tax on billionaires. These wealth tax
revenues probably would add up to tens of billions of dollars spread over several years.
• Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in state income tax revenue
collected from billionaires.
BALLOT LABEL
Fiscal Impact: Temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several
years from wealth tax on billionaires. Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year
in income tax revenue from billionaires.

Memorandum
To: Interested Parties
From: Brian Galle (UC Berkeley), David Gamage (University of Missouri), and Darien
Shanske (UC Davis)1
Re: Analysis of the Impacts of Propositions 41 and 42 on California’s Public Finance
Date: August 20, 2026
Introduction
In this memorandum, we will discuss the potential impacts of Propositions 41 and
42 on current and future initiatives and legislation, as well as on current California
Medicaid tax programs, starting with possible impacts on Proposition 3, the measure on
November’s ballot to extend personal income tax rate increases.
The purpose of the memo is to identify legal risks raised by the propositions that
prudent citizens should be aware of given the high stakes. We are not arguing how a court
should decide these issues and we do not claim that we are offering the best or most
persuasive legal arguments. We do, however, believe that there is a real risk courts could
reach these outcomes.
Our bottom line is that both propositions are poorly drafted in a manner that could
pose serious threats to California’s fiscal future, with the potential to undermine key
spending programs and potentially cause or worsen future budget crises. That is not
surprising. These are deceptive measures that were drafted quickly to trick voters that
support the billionaire wealth tax (Prop 40) into voting for competing measures that could
undermine that tax. The billionaire funders of these initiatives are acting with reckless
disregard for the collateral damage to California’s fiscal system and indeed they may even
benefit from weakening California’s existing taxes affecting the most wealthy.
Executive Summary
• The audit requirements of Proposition 41 could hamstring Proposition 3 (the
teacher-sponsored measure to fund education with taxes on million-dollar earners)
or invalidate it outright.
1 Institutional affiliations are listed for identification purposes only.
2
• The audit requirements of Proposition 41 could similarly hamstring many other
revenue raising measures, such as (for example) a tax on large employers who have
many employees on Medi-Cal.
• The prohibition on easing the state appropriation limit in Proposition 41 could
undermine many existing and proposed taxes to fund California’s contributions to
Medi-Cal, including current MCO taxes and the Hospital Quality Assurance Fee
(HQAF).
• The limitations on taxing personal property in Proposition 42 could impact the
ability of the state to tax capital gains income, whether as part of Proposition 3 or
otherwise.
• The limitation on taxing personal property in Proposition 42 could frustrate any
future attempt to reform California’s Vehicle License Fee, a backbone tool for
financing a wide array of local services.
Proposition 41
Proposition 41 makes two significant changes to California law. First, it adds many
new audit requirements, specifically pre-election audits of programs that would receive
funds from a proposed special tax initiative; and recurring audits, every four years, of
programs receiving moneys from special taxes enacted on or after January 1, 2026,
whether enacted by the Legislature or by initiative.2 Second, the proposition prohibits
collecting any state tax enacted or taking effect on or after January 1, 2026 that is exempted
or excluded from the appropriations limit of Article XIIIB, the so-called Gann limit, whether
the exemption comes from an outside-the-General-Fund special fund whose spending is
not counted or from raising the limit itself. Proposition 41, secs. 3, 4(b). The obvious point
of this second change, hidden deep in the Proposition 41 text, is to nullify Proposition 40.
But both changes would likely weaken California public finance by threatening California’s
ability to raise revenues and fund spending programs.
On the Merits
Prop 41 targets the primary (and, in many cases, the only plausible remaining) way
that state tax policy can be done and that state services can be adequately funded. Any
increase in taxes enacted by the Legislature requires a two-thirds supermajority of each
house.3 Statewide initiatives, by contrast, can raise taxes by majority vote. Not surprisingly,
most major tax policy changes over recent decades have therefore occurred via initiative.
Since voters are unlikely to support tax increases for unspecified purposes, the limits on
2 Prop. 41, Secs. 1, 2.
3 Art. XIIIA, Sec. 3(a).
3
measures adopting taxes for specified purposes tilts the deck against most of those
measures. Even if there were eventually an attempt to change Prop 41 through another
ballot measure, the pre-election audit requirement would still apply to any special tax
initiatives on that ballot.
The audits that Prop 41 would impose are slanted to make it more difficult to adopt
and fund new programs. Consider, for example, that a pre-election audit must consider:
“How the program's costs compare to any analogous programs in the non-government
sector”; and also: “Recommendations on how the program could achieve a budgetary
savings of at least 10% annually.” The audits would thus institutionalize a cost-cutting,
private-sector-comparison framework, and the executive summary of the pre-election
audit would be printed in the voter guide immediately after the Legislative Analyst’s
impartial analysis.4
In sum, every proposed special tax initiative would come before the voters bundled
with an official analysis oriented toward finding savings and private alternatives. These
expensive, burdensome and largely redundant5 requirements would hinder special tax
initiatives, making them more difficult to pass and less effective if passed.
The second provision regarding the Gann limit would double down on what has
proven to be a disastrous set of fiscal policies. The existing Gann limit works by capping
government expenditures over a given two-year period. Excess amounts must be split
between taxpayer rebates and education.6 The cap increases only to the extent of growth in
California population and cost of living.7 Given the increasing demands on the state
government, future uncertainties, and the changing nature of federal assistance, the limit
does not act so much as a ceiling as a vise squeezing out funds for core services.8 For
example, what happens if the state government needs to spend more on (say) wildfires? Or,
4 Sec. 1(e)(2).
5 California law is already full of audit requirements and indeed has a powerful and independent
state auditor (Govt Code 8543 et seq, see especially GC 8546.1) that issues regular,
https://www.auditor.ca.gov/reports/, and, often critical, reports about state operations. See, e.g.,
https://www.auditor.ca.gov/reports/reponses-2025-108-all/. And sometimes the state requires
particular audits. See, e.g., Bus. And Prof. Code 6145(b). As further discussed, the income tax
extensions authorized by Proposition 3 are already subject to audit. Art. XIII, Sec. 36(g).
6 Art. XIIIB, Sec. 2.
7 Art. XIIIB, Secs. 8(e), (f).
8 Making a similar point, here is Jason Sisney (an Assembly budget insider): “Therefore, if revenues
push the state to its Gann limit, non-Proposition 98 programmatic spending (such as annual tax-
supported spending on health and human services (HHS), housing, universities, prisons, state
employees and natural resources programs) probably would have to be cut more in this situation.”
https://jasonsisney.substack.com/p/state-moving-closer-to-its-appropriation
4
what if the state government must spend more to backfill vicious cuts from the federal
government?
The state has hit the Gann limit recently (2022) and is about $30 billion under the

substantial increases in revenue. At that point, the state will be close to the limit. Any

well go over the limit.

which is “a tax that can only be used to fund specific, as opposed to unlimited, purposes”
(according to Prop 41), because the Education Protection Account revenues added by Prop
3 may be used only for specified education and health care purposes. Sec. 4(d) of
Proposition 41; Article XIII, Sec. 36(e) of Proposition 3.
As for whether Proposition 3 was enacted after January 1, 2026, a court could
plausibly find that a tax first approved in 2012 is “enacted” in 2026 when the voters delete
its sunset. The new provision is different than the old in that it will never expire; the post-
2030 tax will exist only because of the 2026 vote; and the adoption of the extension is itself
literally an enactment.9
Thus, Proposition 41 might plausibly be interpreted by courts as applying to

Below are the League of Women Voters of California’s recommendations ** on the propositions appearing on the November 3, 2026 ballot. We base our recommendations on League positions developed through study and member consensus, and the LWVC Board of Directors carefully reviews each measure before taking a position.
**The LWVC Education Fund has provided an unbiased explanation of each ballot measure to help voters make informed decisions. Visit the link at the end of each recommendation for more about each measure.
Proposition 1
VETERANS & AFFORDABLE HOUSING BONDS
Funding from the 2018 bond for broad affordable housing programs has been spent, and there is a corresponding backlog of affordable housing projects stuck waiting for years for financing. Many families in California continue to endure high housing costs, leading to an increase in homelessness and overcrowding. Public subsidy is necessary to provide safe and stable housing for households at the lowest incomes.
Prop 1 authorizes $10 billion in general obligation bonds for the construction, acquisition, rehabilitation, and preservation of affordable housing and for homeownership programs, plus $1.25 billion, also in general obligation bonds, for veteran mortgage assistance through the CalVet Home Loan Program, expected to be repaid from borrowers’ mortgage payments.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 1 Campaign (https://yesonprop1ca.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 1 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-1/)
Proposition 2
SAVE FOR CALIFORNIA’S FUTURE ACT
Proposition 2 will allow California to save more money during strong economic years so it can protect schools and other essential services when revenues fall.
California’s budget can change dramatically from one year to the next. The state relies heavily on personal income taxes, including taxes on capital gains. Capital gains are profits people earn when they sell stocks, businesses, real estate, or other investments. These taxes bring in much more money when financial markets are doing well, but that revenue can disappear quickly during an economic downturn.
Prop 2 would help California prepare for those swings. It would allow the state to build a larger rainy-day fund and require it to save more when capital gains revenues are unusually high. That would give California a stronger financial cushion during recessions, natural disasters, public health emergencies, and other difficult periods.
Saving more during good years can help prevent deep cuts to public services during bad years. It can also reduce the need for emergency borrowing and other painful budget actions.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 2 Campaign (https://www.yesonprop2.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 2 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-2/)
Proposition 3
CHILDREN’S EDUCATION & HEALTH CARE PROTECTION
Proposition 3 would protect funding for schools, health care, and other essential services by keeping California’s current income tax rates on the highest-income 2 percent of taxpayers. Without Prop 3, those rates would fall in 2031, reducing state revenue by an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion each year. Prop 3 would not change anyone’s tax rate today.
About 40 percent of this revenue goes to schools and community colleges. The rest helps fund Medi-Cal and other health and human services, other essential public services, and state budget reserves.
California should not give its highest-income residents a multi-billion-dollar tax cut while schools, health care, and other essential services face serious financial pressure. Prop 3 simply asks the top 2 percent to keep paying the same rates they already pay. The League strongly supports the measure because it protects vital services, helps California weather economic downturns, and keeps the state’s tax system fair.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 3 Campaign (https://www.yesprop3ca.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 3 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-3/)
Proposition 4
CALIFORNIA FAIR ELECTIONS ACT
Elections should be won, not bought. But in California, personal wealth and access to big donors have become unofficial qualifications for public office. Qualified candidates without wealthy networks are often shut out before voters hear their ideas, while candidates and officeholders spend too much time chasing large checks.
Prop 4 gives Californians a way to change that. It lifts California’s near-total ban on public campaign financing and allows the state and local governments to create voluntary programs. The measure creates no financing program and provides no campaign funding by itself. Each jurisdiction decides whether to adopt a program and how to design and pay for it.
Public financing can make small donations matter more, give candidates without personal fortunes a fairer chance to compete, and let them spend more time listening to voters. By reducing the advantage of incumbents, wealthy donors, and special interests, these programs can make elections more open, competitive, and accountable.
They can also open the door to candidates who better reflect California. Latino, Asian American or Pacific Islander, and Black Californians make up nearly two-thirds of our population but remain vastly underrepresented in local government across much of the state. High campaign costs help keep that barrier in place. When voters can choose candidates who understand their communities and reflect their interests, they have more reason to participate.
Prop 4 protects public money. Candidates must show broad grassroots support and agree to spending limits. Money reserved for education, transportation, or public safety cannot be used. Programs cannot favor incumbents or discriminate by party. Public funds cannot pay legal defense costs or fines or repay a candidate’s personal loan to a campaign. Finally, the measure triples the maximum fine for illegal foreign money in California elections.
Prop 4 gives every California community the freedom to build elections where voters have more power and wealthy donors and special interests have less.

Proposition 5
RECALL ELECTION REFORM FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS
California’s recall gives voters a way to remove a corrupt or failed official. It should never become a back door to state office for a replacement candidate propped up by only a small fraction of voters. However, that is exactly what today’s recall rules allow, since the same ballot that decides removal also determines a replacement based on whoever gets the most votes, even if that’s far short of a majority.
Prop 5 fixes a built-in contradiction in the recall process. Voters are asked to remove an officer by majority vote, then hand that same office to a replacement chosen by whomever gets the most votes, often in a field crowded with dozens of candidates and with no requirement that the winner reach half the vote. That’s a loophole that can easily be exploited. In 2021, had the recall against Governor Newsom succeeded, the leading replacement candidate would have taken office with the support of just 28% of recall voters, a stark illustration of exactly this problem.
Prop 5 restores the recall to its proper purpose: deciding whether an official should remain in office. It shuts down that back door with one clean fix: removing the replacement candidate vote from the recall ballot itself. If a recall succeeds, the vacancy is filled through succession, appointment, or a later election decided by real majority support. These are the same rules used to fill any other vacancy in state government. A recalled officer can still run again later. This is a pro-democracy safeguard too – the choice stays with voters rather than being taken away entirely. What Prop 5 rules out is any return to office through appointment, so a recalled officer can only reclaim the seat by winning a real vote.
This is a matter of basic fairness and majority rule. Prop 5 protects accountability while ending a system that can hand power to a candidate most voters never chose.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 5 Campaign (https://fixtherecall.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 5 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-5/)
Proposition 37
LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF NEW HOMES
California must build more homes and make homeownership possible for more families. The League of Women Voters of California has worked toward those goals for decades and supports Prop 1, which would provide $10 billion for affordable housing and homeownership programs and $1.25 billion for veterans’ home loans.
Prop 37 addresses a real barrier: the down payment. But it does so by adding a second mortgage that buyers generally would repay every month.
Prop 37 could help a family buy a home without making it affordable to keep. Buyers generally would repay the Prop 37 loan each month in addition to their first mortgage, property taxes, insurance, repairs, and other costs. Voters would not know the interest rate, loan term, or monthly payment before approving the program.
The program could reinforce racial and economic gaps instead of targeting families facing the greatest barriers . Generations of housing discrimination have left many Black and Latino families with less wealth to draw on, but Prop 37 gives no priority to first-time or first-generation buyers and does not exclude current or former homeowners. Households earning up to twice the area median income could qualify, including some earning more than $300,000 a year, while buyers would still have to provide at least 3 percent of the home price.
The program is not tied to good planning. Assistance could be used only for newly built or newly converted homes, with no requirement that they be near jobs, transit, schools, or services or avoid areas with high transportation, insurance, or natural-hazard costs.
Too much remains undecided. The Legislative Analyst says it is uncertain whether investors would buy the bonds, how the loans would compare in cost with other assistance, or whether the program would result in more homes being built or purchased. The interest rate and repayment terms would be set after the election.
California needs homeownership programs that lower families’ total costs, confront racial barriers to building wealth, and support strong communities. Prop 37 does not meet that test.

Unbiased Explanation: Prop 37 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-37/)
Proposition 38
BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH
Medical research can save lives, but Prop 38 is the wrong way to fund it. It would authorize $8.4 billion in borrowing for immunology and immunotherapy research and require the state to make $500 million to $600 million in annual debt payments for about 20 years. Those payments would come from the General Fund, which also pays for schools, health care, and other public services.
Borrowing is a poor way to pay for ongoing scientific research. Bonds are best suited to long-lived investments such as buildings and infrastructure. With interest, the Legislative Analyst estimates Prop 38 would cost about 10 percent more, after adjusting for inflation, than paying for the research up front.
Prop 38 would lock billions of dollars into one field of research for years to come. About half of the money would go to a single UC-affiliated research institute and the other half to a grant program, with at least $4.2 billion reserved for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research. Scientific opportunities and public health needs change. State funding should be able to respond to those changes rather than locking billions of dollars into one field of research through a ballot measure.
Research royalties are no reason to take on $8.4 billion in debt. When voters approved $3 billion for stem-cell research in 2004, supporters pointed to royalties and millions in new state revenue. By 2022, CIRM reported only $15.6 million in its licensing and royalties fund from royalty payments. Prop 38 again points to research-generated revenue as a way to offset public costs, but the Legislative Analyst says the amount and timing are unknown.
California can support important medical research without committing taxpayers to decades of debt and restricting future choices about where limited public dollars can do the most good.

Proposition 39
PROHIBITS VOTING WITHOUT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED ID
Prop 39 is a partisan power grab to further President Trump’s voter suppression efforts. It is based on lies about our elections. Prop 39 is intended to make it harder to vote and easier for politicians to decide which voters count. Right-wing billionaires spent millions to put it on the ballot.
California’s elections are already secure. Voters swear to citizenship under penalty of perjury, and officials verify identity at registration, check the rolls in person, and match every mail ballot signature.
A new registration hurdle. Millions of existing voters could be forced to effectively re-register to “designate” a government ID for mail voting, like a driver’s license or Social Security number.
Identity theft risk. You would be required to put the last four digits of that sensitive ID number on the outside of your ballot envelope – next to your name, address, and signature.
Valid ballots thrown out. Your mailed ballot would not be counted if the number you wrote didn’t match the “designated” number. One wrong digit or a blank field could sink a valid ballot, with no guaranteed notice or chance to fix it. Texas tried this and rejected one in eight mail ballots. Those voters were less likely to vote again.
An ID check every time you vote in person. You would have to show a government-issued ID every time, even after officials verified who you are. Most voters turned away under similar laws elsewhere had qualifying ID, just not on them.
A modern-day poll tax. A “free” ID is not free. Getting one costs transportation, childcare, time off work, and fees for the paperwork behind it. Seniors, students, low-income workers, voters with disabilities, and voters of color are hit hardest.
Valid ID still must match. Nearly 30 percent of U.S. adults have changed their name, 94 percent of them women. Californians who took a new name at marriage, and transgender voters whose documents lag may hold valid ID and be turned away anyway.
Bad data and wrongful purges. Citizenship checks would likely run through untrustworthy federal databases that wrongly flag eligible citizens to purge them from voter rolls.
Longer lines and slower results. Extra ID checks and flagged ballots add delay, and the lawsuits would stretch it further, handing election deniers more time to spread lies.
Hundreds of millions of dollars every year. New systems, staffing, free ID cards, audits, and lawsuits, all paid for while California already has budget problems.
Don’t let President Trump and right-wing billionaires decide whose vote counts.

Authors

Document Type
Article
Publication Date
9-2026
Abstract
This memorandum discusses the possible collateral damage that Propositions 41 and 42 (on the ballot in California on November 3, 2026) might cause. The two propositions were concocted very quickly by billionaires in order to trick voters that will vote for Proposition 40 (the billionaire tax) also to vote for these propositions that are designed to undermine the billionaire tax.
The basic trick is that these propositions have plausible seeming veneers but hide a poison pill that aims to frustrate the functioning of the billionaire tax. The veneers are “plausible seeming” because they address problems that are not problems. For example, Prop 42 protects retirement assets when there is no threat to them – certainly not from Prop 40 (which exempts them).
But this memo focuses on an issue other than their deceptiveness and general disrespect for the democratic process. Because these propositions were drafted so quickly and poorly as poison pills for one tax measure, they could, if passed, impact many other vital policy initiatives. Some possible negative impacts include.
· The audit requirements of Proposition 41 could hamstring Proposition 3 (the teacher-sponsored measure to fund education with taxes on million-dollar earners) or invalidate it outright.
· The audit requirements of Proposition 41 could similarly hamstring many other revenue raising measures, such as (for example) a tax on large employers who have many employees on Medi-Cal.
· The limitations on taxing personal property in Proposition 42 could impact the ability of the state to tax capital gains income, whether as part of Proposition 3 or otherwise.
· The limitation on taxing personal property in Proposition 42 could frustrate any future attempt to reform California’s Vehicle License Fee, a backbone tool for financing a wide array of local services.

temporary and will not continue post-2030 unless voters remove its sunset. Notably,
Proposition 42 does not specify how its exemption clause applies to extensions of this sort.
Taxpayers thus may be able to argue that Proposition 41 prohibits the tax imposed
by Proposition 3 because the latter is a tax “on the ownership or control” of property.
Because Proposition 42 never defines “ownership or control,” its protected category
potentially encompasses all income-producing personal property; it is a longstanding
income tax principle that income from a property is taxed “to the one who controls it.” For
example, consider the current treatment of stock options one earns as part of one’s job.
Such options are treated as labor income and, if exercised years later, a formula is used to
assess how much of their appreciation should be attributed to California.22 A court might
21 California broadly conforms to the positive tax benefits given to retirement savings by the federal
tax code. See generally Ca. Rev. and Tax Code 17501 et seq. Further, any reduction in these benefits
granted by California tax law would require a 2/3 supermajority. Cal. Constit. Art. XIIIA, Sec. 3(a).
Proposition 40 does not change any of this and, in fact, explicitly exempts true retirement assets.
See Proposition 40, Proposed Section 50303(c)(7).
22 See Cal. Code Regs. tit. 18, section 17951-5(b).
9
treat the post-2030 taxation of that option appreciation, or even of capital gains generally,
as a tax on the ownership or control of “financial assets” that is grandfathered only through
2030.
Proposition 42 could also arguably void Proposition 3 entirely if Proposition 42 gets
more votes. Proposition 42 has a sweeping conflicts provision (Sec. 5(a)) that could be read
to trigger if Proposition 3 were interpreted as permitting any form of taxation prohibited
by Proposition 42. Note further in regard to this that California adjudicators have recently
read formal tax terms, such as “unitary business,”23 “gross receipts,”24 and “agricultural
business activity,”25 in ways the drafters of those terms plainly did not anticipate, and
“personal property” could well follow a similar pattern.26
Moreover, Proposition 42 separately prohibits a post-2025 tax that “operates
retroactively to result in tax liability based on conduct, activities, or a status that occurred
or was present prior to the effective date” of the law. Sec. 2(a)(1). A court could hold that
this clause applies where post-2030 taxes fall on gains that accrued, or on equity
compensation earned, in earlier years. If so, the post-2030 rates could not be collected with
respect to income deemed attributable to earlier years, such as gain reflecting appreciation
that accrued before 2031 or compensation from services performed earlier. This could
substantially undermine the revenue-raising capacity of Prop 3. And a ruling of this kind
would also satisfy the second trigger of Proposition 42's conflicts provision, and so (as
discussed above), could result in all of Prop 3 being nullified.
Other Taxes
Proposition 42’s restrictions as to the taxation of other assets are very broad and
might impact a variety of current taxes or those that might reasonably be proposed. For
example, consider the bar on taxing “personal property.” This would, on its face, seem to
apply to the Vehicle License Fee, which is a tax on personal property.27 This fee is so
important to local governments that it was guaranteed to them by Prop 30 (Art. XIII, Sec.
36(b)(2)) and the allocation of its revenues to local governments is protected elsewhere in

24 Appeal of Microsoft Corp. and Subsidiaries, 2024-OTA-130 (Cal. Off. Tax App. July 27, 2023).
25 Smithfield Packaged Meats Corp. v. California Franchise Tax Board, No. 21STCV39637 (Cal. Super.
Ct. 2026) (final statement of decision).
26 We do not mean to imply here that we agree with these decisions, but the fact remains that a
certain rigid formalism seems appealing to the California judiciary sometimes.
27 Now, there is some complexity here because the VLF was held in 1936 not to be a tax on personal
property but a tax on a privilege. See Ingels v. Riley, 5 Cal. 2d. 154 (1936). But Prop 42 would seem
to apply to a privilege tax.
10
the constitution, which requires the state to backfill localities if the rate falls below 0.65%
(Art. XI, Sec. 15). Given that the current rate of the VLF (0.65%) is lower than the rate that
it was long before, and the sound policy reasons why the rate should at least be the same as
the rate for real property (1%), Prop 42 will interfere with the Legislature or the people
increasing this tax. While Prop 13 doesn’t leave much room for maneuver on real estate
taxes, Proposition 42 would constrict that freedom even further by apparently prohibiting
any future state changes, absent a constitutional amendment.
Retroactivity
Prop 42’s limit on retroactive taxes will also make future tax reform harder and less
effective. Again, the only real policy payoff of this provision is to sink the billionaire tax; the
Due Process Clause of the 14th Amendment of the federal constitution already bars states
from engaging in unreasonable retroactive taxation.28 In many cases good tax policy
requires that new taxes apply to at least some transactions that happened before the tax
was adopted. New taxes are often effective prior to enactment date in order to prevent
arbitrage or other evasive transactions before the tax can go into effect. Other retroactive
measures may simply fix a mistake or close off an unintended tax shelter that taxpayers
have been exploiting, as in the leading Supreme Court cases. In other cases, going back to
sometime before enactment of the tax may ensure a more accurate measure of the tax base.
For example, the federal Tax Cuts and Jobs Act did just that.29 Having a tax change be
retroactive to the start of the year is also a way to start raising revenue immediately should
that be desired. All of these practices are longstanding and common and flow from the
states’ inherent power to control their own revenue systems.
Prop 42’s retroactivity bar could also further complicate health care financing
legislation. Provider fee statutes are sometimes written so that they apply to periods that
begin before enactment, with collection following once federal approval arrives. A post-
2025 statute with this structure could thus be threatened by Prop 42, Sec. 2(a)(1). The
existing hospital fee framework predates 2026 and thus has a grandfather defense
shielding it from these threats,30 but this defense does not protect future bills that may
reach backward, and so drafters will face new constraints and risks if Prop 42 passes.
Conclusion
California’s public finance rules are already exceptionally baroque. This irrational
opacity is particularly harmful considering that California’s underlying tax bases have not

29 26 USC 965(a)(1).
30 Sec. 2(b).
11
been substantially reformed for a century and the state has many urgent needs. Both
Propositions 41 and 42 add even more complexity to this rickety system, which, by itself,
should be avoided. As it is, the complicated and vague new rules that would be imposed by
Propositions 41 and 42 are likely to make it much harder to finance all manner of public
goods going forward.

90% of the revenue to health care, with the remaining 10% going to education, food assistance, and administration of the wealth tax. That could deliver tens of billions to the safety net when families are losing both.
The measure also confronts a deeper problem the League cannot ignore. The wealthiest American households pay a lower total effective tax rate than the whole population, largely because business wealth produces little taxable income. As of September 2025, roughly 900 American billionaires held nearly double the wealth of the entire bottom half of the country. Inequality on that scale demands that solutions like wealth taxes get serious consideration.
On the con side, Prop 40 makes budget decisions at the ballot box, locking the proceeds into an earmarked fund. The Legislature could choose how to spend within those categories but could not redirect the money to other needs. A one-time tax is also only a stopgap for programs that need funding every year. Furthermore, the tax rests on only a few hundred people. Of these, six billionaires reportedly left the state before the January 1, 2026, cutoff, potentially erasing more than one-quarter of the proponents’ projected $100 billion revenue. It should be noted that the government estimates only tens of billions of dollars raised over several years and says the amount is highly uncertain. The government also estimates that state revenue could be reduced by less than $1 billion per year.
The deeper fear is behavioral: that the tax pushes billionaires out after they pay and deters others from ever coming. The government offers only the broad estimate that state revenue could be reduced by below $1 billion per year. On the other hand, some research finds that tax-driven migration among the wealthy is modest, and Silicon Valley’s ecosystem is not easily traded away.
The human need is urgent and asking those most able to pay to fill a hole the federal government created is a fair demand. But the tax mechanism limits legislative flexibility for allocating money where it is most crucial and raises the risk of taxpayer flight. Because we have strong positions on both sides of this measure, the League takes a neutral position on Prop 40.

Proposition 41
LIMITS NEW STATE TAXES & REQUIRES SPECIAL TAX AUDITS
Prop 41 would put revenue from new state taxes under the Gann Limit’s rigid constitutional spending cap, making it harder to fund essential services and respond to changing needs. It would apply to any state tax enacted or taking effect on or after January 1, 2026.
The League opposed the Gann Initiative in 1979 because its spending limit was too inflexible to assure adequate government services in an uncertain future. Prop 41 would extend that constraint to new tax revenue. This is especially concerning for voter-approved initiatives, which generally cannot be changed by the Legislature without another vote of the people.
Prop 41 would also require audits of programs funded by new or increased special taxes, including programs such as public campaign financing that may not receive General Fund support. If a new tax excluded its revenue from the Gann Limit, the state could not impose, collect, or enforce it. And when the state is at or near the limit, Prop 41 could prevent all the revenue voters approved for a specific purpose from being spent on that purpose.
The audits would add state costs, estimated by the Legislative Analyst’s Office in the low millions of dollars annually and growing over time. The General Fund would pay for a pre-election audit if an initiative failed to qualify or is rejected by voters. New programs could also be difficult to evaluate before they exist.
Prop 41 is also designed to prevail over a conflicting initiative on the same ballot. If both Prop 40, the Billionaire Tax measure, and Prop 41 pass and Prop 41 receives more “yes” votes, courts could find that they conflict and prevent Prop 40 from becoming law. Litigation could delay a final determination.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 41 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-41/)
Proposition 42
LIMITS NEW STATE TAXES ON PERSONAL PROPERTY
Prop 42 would lock broad new restrictions on state taxing power into the California Constitution, limiting California’s ability to respond to future needs.
The ban goes far beyond retirement savings . It would prohibit new state taxes on the ownership or control of a wide range of personal property, including stocks and other financial assets, business interests, art, intellectual property, retirement accounts, and other savings and assets.
Prop 42 would limit certain retroactive state taxes. This includes new taxes based on conduct, activity, or status that occurred before the tax took effect.
The restrictions would be difficult to change. Because they would be in the Constitution, changing them in the future would require another vote of the people. A tax that does not make sense today may be appropriate under different circumstances in the future.
Prop 42 is also designed to prevail over a conflicting initiative on the same ballot. If both Prop 40, the Billionaire Tax measure, and Prop 42 pass and Prop 42 receives more “yes” votes, courts could find that the measures conflict and prevent Prop 40 from becoming law. A court challenge could delay a final determination.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 42 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-42/)
Proposition 43
LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES
Prop 43 would make it harder for communities to raise revenue for public services by allowing a minority of voters to block local tax measures. It would amend the Constitution to require a two-thirds vote for any new, increased, or extended special tax proposed by local voters through the initiative process. A simple majority keeps these decisions with most voters and gives communities more flexibility to respond to changing needs.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
No on Prop 43 Campaign (https://www.noprop43ca.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 43 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-43/)
Proposition 44
90% HEALTH CARE SPENDING FOR NONPROFIT SAFETY-NET CLINICS
Prop 44 could reduce access to health care for Californians who already have the fewest options. It would impose a rigid spending requirement on nonprofit safety-net clinics serving low-income and uninsured patients. Clinics that cannot meet the requirement could face substantial penalties or even close, shifting patients to other public safety-net providers and increasing public costs.
Prop 44 would require affected clinics to spend at least 90% of their annual revenue on health care services. Clinics currently report spending an average of about 80%, although the percentage varies. The Attorney General would decide which expenses count toward the 90% requirement, using existing federal reports as a starting point.
Clinics falling below 90% would have to pay the state the amount of the shortfall. Although they could seek a temporary waiver or recover the money if they later comply, the financial pressure could threaten clinics serving communities that already have limited access to care.
A rule intended to direct more money to patient care should not put the safety net itself at risk. Prop 44 could worsen health disparities rather than reduce them.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
No on Prop 44 Campaign (https://noprop44.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 44 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-44/)
Proposition 45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS
The League of Women Voters of California has always recognized the need for the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) mandated environmental reviews of projects to create new housing, education, health, and public safety facilities, plus clean energy, transportation, and water projects to determine potential environmental impacts and mitigation measures to reduce adverse impacts.
At the same time, the League is aware that CEQA has been used to delay, if not completely derail, large projects. The League has supported some streamlining of CEQA requirements. But the process overhaul of CEQA proposed by Prop 45 goes too far.
Prop 45 is a long, very detailed statute that would significantly modify CEQA for specified “essential projects” to enforce strict timelines, constrain public participation with unreasonable timelines, eliminate key environmental analyses, and more. It addresses potentially very large-scale infrastructure projects, and their subsidiary components with the same time constraints as smaller “essential projects,” increasing the probability of rushed studies, incomplete analyses, lack of feasible alternatives, poor interagency coordination, less public participation, and decisions that are done in haste to meet the required timelines without considering the full consequences of the proposed “essential project.”
Statutory exemptions and expedited processes are in place, some of which the League supported, making Proposition 45 unnecessary and flawed with this prescriptive process and inflated promises. Further Prop 45 reduces opportunity for public engagement. Finally, voters are being asked to pass this long, detailed statute in a ballot initiative. Making changes or adjustments to this law would be difficult: legislative amendments would require a two-thirds vote of each house and would have to be consistent with and further the purposes of the measure; broader changes would have to go back to the voters.

The research base is solid. The OC Register and Newsom's counterarguments need closer examination. Collateral damage claims may be overstated by tax law professors who designed wealth taxes. Their memo is advocacy-tinged. They identify risks rather than predict court outcomes.

Speculative collateral damage should be discounted. The clear intended effects are the ban on new ownership taxes, retroactivity limits, and the poison pill versus Prop 40 outcome. Possible litigation risks around VLF increases, capital gains, and Prop 3 were not flagged as primary effects by the LAO.

The LAO is the more neutral source. It forecasts only a possibility that tax revenues will not rise as much in the future and that raising taxes may be somewhat harder. It does not claim existing income taxes or VLF would be invalidated. The grandfather clause protects taxes in effect, imposed, and first collected before December 31, 2025. VLF and income tax are already protected. Prop 3 extends an existing tax, so courts would likely grandfather it, though litigation risk remains.

The drafting is broadly worded and liberally construed, so some litigation risk is genuine. The core policy case for voting NO is strong: the problem it claims to solve is largely fictional. No active proposal taxes ordinary retirement accounts. Prop 40 already exempts pensions and retirement accounts, except for very large Roth IRAs over $10 million.

Past wealth tax bills died in committee and targeted billionaires, not middle-class 401ks. CalMatters confirms no active proposals tax those accounts on the ballot or in the Legislature.

The measure is a poison pill rather than a good-government reform. It was drafted and funded by billionaires to nullify Prop 40 even if voters approve it. Its "protect your retirement" ads omit the billionaire involvement. Voters can simply vote no on Prop 40 to stop it. The unique effect of 42 is a permanent constitutional restriction that could override a majority vote for 40.

A constitutional lock-in is costly. California already has Prop 13, supermajority tax requirements, the Gann limit, and no estate tax. A broad ban on new taxes for all personal property permanently removes fiscal tools. The League of Women Voters, SPUR, the San Francisco Chronicle, the Sacramento Bee, and the Mercury News/BANG all oppose the measure because it shackles the state's fiscal future. Even papers that dislike the wealth tax itself, such as the Sacramento Bee, vote no on both propositions. The retroactivity ban is redundant with due process and overbroad.

The retroactivity ban would interfere with ordinary tax administration. It would block year-of-enactment effective dates and anti-abuse retroactivity. The 365-day emergency exception applies only to legislative statutes, not initiatives.

Fiscal context matters. Federal cuts to Medi-Cal and food assistance make preserving revenue options more valuable. The LAO notes that 42 could reduce future tax revenues without any offsetting revenue or service benefit.

Rewarding deceptive ballot measures with conflict clauses encourages more of them. The measure asks voters to protect retirement while its text secretly nullifies another proposition.

Wealth taxes have real design problems, but that is a reason to vote no on Prop 40. It does not justify constitutionalizing a sweeping ban sold under false pretenses.

Newsom supports the measure because he fears a wealth tax precedent. That concern is reasonable, but the ban is broader than simply blocking wealth taxes on billionaires. The advertising is also dishonest. A narrower approach could have restricted only wealthy individuals or required voter approval for any new personal property ownership tax.

Firefighters and trades support it. Their argument that wealth taxes would lead to retirement taxes is the classic tax slippery slope.
